Native control appearance follows the [Studio control design rules](Design/Controls.md):
visible action surfaces and states, themed fields, colored vector-axis badges and overflow indicators.
Open or create a project

Use **Create new project** on the welcome screen, or choose **File > Open Project** to open an existing project. AdaScript projects use `.ada` source files. Projects with native Swift code also use Swift Package Manager.
Explore and edit

The Project Navigator shows project files. Select a source file to edit it, or a `.ascn` scene to open the scene viewport. Use the scene hierarchy to select entities and the Inspector to edit their components. Use **File > New File** to create files and **File > Import Assets** to bring assets into the project.
Use **File > Save** to save the active document, or **File > Save All** to save all documents. The Code menu includes tab actions and editor font size controls.
Import and place a 3D model

Use **File > Import Assets** or drop a `.glb`, `.gltf` or MagicaVoxel `.vox` into the project navigator.
Models open in a 3D preview with camera navigation, mesh/material/skin counts,
and a named animation picker with Play/Pause. Preview framing fits the model;
placing it in a scene preserves its original scale.

Open the destination `.ascn` scene, then open the model and choose
**Add to Scene…**. Select the destination from the open scenes. The new entity
stores a portable resource reference, so Save, reopening, duplicate and undo/redo
retain the model without copying imported nodes into the authored scene file.
The selected preview clip and playback setting become the entity's initial
animation settings.

Alternatively, add **Imported Model 3D** from the entity palette or add a
**Model 3D** component to an existing entity. In the Inspector, choose a project
model, enter a clip name shown in its preview, and set **Play animation** and
**Loop animation**. Imported nodes/materials are instantiated in both the scene
viewport and Play. Each placed model has its own animation player.

glTF imports with external buffers or textures are copied into a new model folder
with those dependencies. Keep dependencies beneath the source model's directory;
remote URLs and references escaping that directory are rejected. Missing files
fail the bundle import. Repeated imports create another bundle without replacing
the original. Imported materials are preserved. Imported meshes/rigs remain source
assets; editable animation clips are stored separately as described below.
Edit bone animation

Select a Model 3D entity and open **Animator → Bone Keyframes**. Extract an editable
copy of an imported clip or create a clip from the rig's rest pose. Select bones,
tracks and timeline keys to edit translation, rotation, scale or morph weights.
Preview the model, use Undo/Redo, then explicitly **Save** the `.animlib` resource.
Autosave and tab switches retain animation drafts without writing them.
**Save and Bind** attaches a saved compatible library through the scene's own history;
the Skeletal Graph can then select its qualified clips. See
[Editing bone animation](AnimationAuthoring.md) for key commands, conflict recovery
and the shared agent/Studio Tools API. The offline **Authoring skeletal animation**
guide also covers Swift library construction and runtime graph references.
MagicaVoxel models

A `.vox` file is imported and placed like any other model: it opens in the 3D
preview, **Add to Scene…** creates a **Model 3D** entity, and the model appears in
the scene viewport and in Play. A voxel file is self-contained, so import simply
copies it (repeated imports get a new name instead of overwriting).

The scene is imported as an entity hierarchy that keeps the MagicaVoxel node names
and transforms, so parts such as an arm can be picked and animated separately.
Keyframed transforms and models with several frames animate; the preview header
shows the frame count and rate, and Play/Pause controls the voxel timeline.
**Play animation** on the Model 3D component decides whether it starts playing.
MagicaVoxel is right-handed with Z up and the engine is left-handed with Y up,
so the import swaps those axes; a model keeps the look of MagicaVoxel's front view.

The Model 3D inspector has three voxel settings that apply to `.vox` sources only
and stay at their defaults for other formats:

• **Voxel size** (default 0.1) is the edge length of one voxel in world units.
• **Merge static voxels** merges parts without animation into one mesh. This lowers
  the draw count and removes hidden faces between parts, but merged parts can no
  longer be picked separately.
• **Voxel animation fps** (default 30) is the playback rate of MagicaVoxel frames.

Voxel materials are not imported yet: colors come from the palette and the model
uses one diffuse material. The model tools of the AI agent work with glTF only.
Shape terrain

Open a scene and choose **Terrain** in the viewport toolbar. In the dock, choose
**Mesh Terrain** to join a static model to the ground or **Heightfield** to sculpt
height samples with Raise, Lower, Smooth or Flatten. Inspect the triangles with
the 3D viewport's **Wireframe** mode. See the Terrain guide for a
worked join, heightfield tools, saved versions, and collision.
Build and run

Choose **Build > Build Project** to build the project. **Build > Run** runs the active scene inside the editor when a scene is selected; otherwise it runs the selected target. **Build > Stop** stops the current operation. Build Output and Problems show progress and diagnostics.
Settings
Open **Settings** for editor preferences and **Project > Project Settings** for project configuration. Project Dependencies and Swift Package Tasks are available in the Project menu.
Read documentation offline

Choose **Help > AdaEngine Documentation** or use the **Documentation** button. These guides ship with the editor and are available without a network connection or an engine checkout. Search matches article titles and contents. Use the article list, section links, and Back and Forward buttons to navigate. Code examples and complete articles can be copied.
The offline library contains hand-written engine and AdaScript guides. Generated API reference pages and external websites are not included. External links are marked as requiring internet.
Start scripting
Read Getting Started with AdaScript, then AdaScript Language and AdaScript ECS.
Interactive agent forms

On macOS, ACP agents can stream native AdaUI forms and previews directly into
Agent Chat using the advertised A2UI catalog. Ask for an NPC configuration form,
edit the controls, and submit after the agent's turn finishes. The current values
return to the same conversation, and the agent can generate an editable preview.
**Open in UI Designer** creates a new `.ui` asset under `Assets/UI/AgentPreviews`;
refine it through the normal designer, undo/redo, and save workflow. Local form
edits persist with the chat. Invalid updates retain the last working form and
show an interface error; interrupted forms remain disabled until refreshed.
The separate iPhone chat path is not connected to these cards yet.
Bringing simple and powerful game engine for your awesome games.

Overview

Ada is a modern, open-source game engine written in Swift, designed for building 2D and 3D games with simplicity and performance in mind. Its architecture leverages the Entity Component System (ECS) paradigm, enabling developers to create games and interactive experiences using a modular and scalable approach.

Ada provides a suite of built-in features, including:
• High-level rendering system supporting 2D and 3D graphics
• Physics, animation, input handling, audio, and UI systems
• Asset management pipeline and streamlined workflows
• Cross-platform support across Apple platforms and Linux
• Hot-reload capabilities for assets and scripts
• Modern Swift API with async/await, property wrappers, and result builders

With Ada, both beginners and experienced Swift developers can build games rapidly, focusing on gameplay instead of low-level boilerplate. Extensive documentation and tutorials make it easy to get started, from setting up your first scene to advanced gameplay mechanics.

Ada is actively developed, and contributions from the community are welcome.
For more details and guides, check out the tutorials below.

This guide covers two scenarios:
• Development build for working on Ada itself.
• Using Ada as a dependency in your own app.
Requirements

• Swift 6.2 toolchain
• Xcode 26.3 (macOS) or Visual Studio Code with the Swift extension
• Git
Development build
1\. Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/AdaEngine/AdaEngine.git
cd AdaEngine
2\. WebGPU (first build). If you plan to use WebGPU, run the tint build plugin once (this executes `Plugins/WebGPUTintPlugin/WebGPUTintPlugin.swift`):
swift package plugin build-tint
This command downloads the Dawn/Tint sources from GitHub and builds the `tint` binary. SwiftPM will ask to allow network access for the plugin. Confirm the prompt to proceed.
3\. Open `Package.swift` in Xcode 26.3, or build from the command line:
swift build
4\. Run tests:
swift test --parallel
5\. (Optional) Run SwiftLint if you have it installed locally:
swiftlint --config .swiftlint.yml
Using Ada in your app
Xcode

1\. Open your project in Xcode 26.3.
2\. Go to `File > Add Packages...`.
3\. Enter the package URL: `https://github.com/AdaEngine/AdaEngine.git`.
4\. Choose a version range and add the package to your app target.
5\. Import the module in your code:
import AdaEngine
Swift Package Manager
Add Ada to your `Package.swift`:
Replace `X.Y.Z` with the latest release tag.
If your app enables WebGPU, run the tint build plugin once in the Ada package directory before the first build:
swift package plugin build-tint
SwiftPM will ask to allow network access for the plugin. Confirm the prompt to let it download the Dawn/Tint sources.
Exporting a Web app
Ada includes an experimental WebAssembly export command for browser-hosted games.
Requirements:

• Swift 6.3.2 release toolchain.
• `swift-6.3.2-RELEASE_wasm` installed with `swift sdk install`.
• A game executable product that depends on `AdaEngine`. Add `AdaWeb` if the app needs browser-specific helpers.

Swift.org documents the current WebAssembly SDK installation flow at:
https://www.swift.org/documentation/articles/wasm-getting-started.html
Export a package product:

swift package --allow-writing-to-package-directory \
  export-web \
  --product MyGame \
  --output dist/web
If several WASM SDKs are installed, pass the SDK id explicitly:

swift package --allow-writing-to-package-directory \
  export-web \
  --product MyGame \
  --swift-sdk swift-6.3.2-RELEASE_wasm

The plugin emits `index.html`, `main.js`, `runtime.mjs`, the built `.wasm`, `package.json`, `ada-web-manifest.json`, `ada-resource-manifest.json`, copied SwiftPM resource bundles, and copies a package-level `Assets` directory when present. Use `npm install && npm run serve` in the output directory to serve the bundle locally.

AdaUI reconciles a new view tree against the mounted `ViewNode` tree. A node is preserved only when the new node and old node describe the same identity and the new node can update the old node. Preserved nodes keep their `@State`, focus state, in-flight animation controllers, layers, and other node-local runtime state. Recreated nodes start with fresh runtime state.
Identity Model
For every sibling list, AdaUI resolves identity in this order:

1\. Explicit identity from `.id(_:)` or `ForEach` data IDs.
2\. Structural identity from result-builder constructs, including the active branch of `if` / `else`.
3\. Structural sibling position for children without explicit IDs.
Explicit IDs are scoped to the current sibling list. IDs must be unique within that list; duplicate IDs are ambiguous and are not a stable state-preservation contract.

`.id(_:)` binds a node to a hashable identity value. If the value is unchanged, AdaUI may move that node to a different sibling index and preserve its runtime state. If the value changes, AdaUI treats the view as a different node and recreates it.
The view type still participates in matching. A node with the same explicit ID but an incompatible concrete node type is recreated instead of being updated in place.
`ForEach`
`ForEach` wraps each generated child in an explicit identity:

• `ForEach(data)` uses each element's `Identifiable.id`.
• `ForEach(data, id: keyPath)` uses the key-path value.
• `ForEach(0..<n)` is position-based and is intended for constant ranges.

Reordering identified data preserves the child nodes associated with those IDs, so row `@State`, focus, and animations follow the data item rather than the visual index. Inserting or deleting an item only creates or removes nodes for the affected IDs.
Conditional Branches

`if` / `else` branches add a structural branch discriminator. This prevents state from moving between two branches that happen to produce the same view type at the same sibling position. Switching from one branch to the other recreates that branch's node; explicit IDs are still scoped by the active branch structure.
`@State` Properties

`@State` storage belongs to the preserved view node and to the exact property wrapper slot inside that view. The slot key includes the wrapper's declaration order among state-like wrappers, its reflected property label, and its value type.

Renaming a `@State` property creates a new storage slot. Reordering `@State` properties also creates new slots for the moved wrappers. Adding or removing a state wrapper preserves only wrappers whose slot key is unchanged.

This rule intentionally resets state after source-level declaration edits rather than migrating values between properties. It prevents a rebuild from moving state between different properties or between different view instances. Dynamic or reorderable view instances still need `.id(_:)` or `ForEach(_:id:)` so the owning view node has stable identity.
Unkeyed Children

Children without explicit IDs are matched by structural sibling position. AdaUI uses common-prefix and common-suffix matching for unkeyed runs, which preserves unaffected nodes around an insertion or deletion in the middle. Reordering unkeyed siblings has no semantic identity signal, so state is not guaranteed to follow a particular data item; use `.id(_:)` or `ForEach(_:id:)` for reorderable content.
Mixed Keyed And Unkeyed Children

In a mixed sibling list, keyed nodes are matched by ID first. The remaining unkeyed nodes are reconciled by their structural order with the same prefix/suffix rules. This keeps static unkeyed content stable around keyed inserts, deletes, and reorders, while still requiring explicit IDs for dynamic reorderable items.
Run Ada apps in visionOS Shared Space using the existing `WindowGroup` scene model.
Overview

Ada's first visionOS milestone is windowed rendering. Apps launch as normal visionOS windows backed by UIKit scenes, `MTKView`, and the Metal render backend. Existing apps that use `WindowGroup` do not need a new public API for this mode.
Windowed mode intentionally does not create a Full Space, stereo renderer, ARKit session, or `CompositorServices.LayerRenderer` surface. Those belong to a later immersive rendering milestone.

title: Known issues and how to debug SPM targets

blocks.text: Xcode Instruments: "Required kernel recording resources are in use by another document"
When profiling an SPM project (without an xcodeproj) in Instruments, you may see a message about kernel recording resources being in use, even when no other Instruments documents are open.

**Cause:** The message is misleading. The real cause is that the binary does not have the `get-task-allow` entitlement. SPM does not distinguish between “release” and “profiling,” so profiling uses a release build without this entitlement.
**Solution:** Re-sign the binary with the `get-task-allow` entitlement before launching Instruments.

1\. Open your scheme (Cmd-Shift-,).
2\. In **Profile → Pre-actions**, add a Pre-action.
3\. Set the shell to `/bin/zsh`.
4\. Paste the re-sign script below (the `=(...)` syntax is zsh process substitution):

# For Instruments, re-sign binary with get-task-allow entitlement
codesign -s - -v -f --entitlements =(echo -n '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "https://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
    <dict>
        <key>com.apple.security.get-task-allow</key>
        <true/>
    </dict>
</plist>') ${TARGET_BUILD_DIR}/${PRODUCT_NAME}
See also: Solving "Required kernel recording resources..." in Instruments (Rob Napier).

links.title: Solving "Required kernel recording resources..." in Instruments

blocks.text: The script is stored in `.swiftpm/xcode/xcshareddata/xcschemes/<schemename>.xcscheme`. The pre-action runs only for Profile, so it does not affect normal builds.
**Note:** Pre-action scripts do not receive `SRCROOT`; if the script fails, Xcode will not show details—check Console.app for logs.

Write gameplay systems in AdaScript while keeping entity filtering and access planning in AdaEngine's native ECS.
Overview

AdaScript is AdaEngine's scripting layer for gameplay and ECS integration. Its source files use the `.ada` extension. The current implementation uses an embedded language runtime, while the public API, diagnostics, and tooling consistently present AdaScript concepts.
Annotations are not only syntax. AdaEngine resolves every query into native archetypes and component columns and publishes its component access to the scheduler.
Use AdaScript for gameplay rules that benefit from quick iteration. Keep rendering backends, custom data structures, and other low-level or performance-critical facilities in Swift.

AdaEditor projects configure automatic script discovery by default. For an existing Swift package, follow Getting Started with AdaScript to enable the build plugin and register the generated script plugins.

Add an `.ada` file to an AdaEngine executable and run its systems without manually loading each script.
Overview
AdaEngine provides two ways to install AdaScript plugins:

• **Automatic discovery** embeds every `.ada` file in an executable target at
  build time and generates one plugin backed by one target-level script module.
• **Manual loading** creates an `AdaScriptPlugin` from source text or a file URL at runtime.
AdaEditor-created projects use automatic discovery. Use manual loading when scripts live outside the Swift target, come from a downloaded package, or need explicit error handling.
Create a script
Add `Movement.ada` anywhere below the executable target's source directory, for example:

Sources/MyGame/
├── main.swift
└── Scripts/
    └── Movement.ada
Declare a system and its query with annotations:
AdaEngine discovers `@system` and `@query` metadata and calls `update(context)` whenever the selected scheduler runs.
Enable automatic discovery
Expose `AdaScriptBuildPlugin` to your executable target in `Package.swift`:
> Important: Choose a version requirement appropriate for your project instead of a branch dependency when consuming a released AdaEngine version.

The build plugin finds `.ada` files through SwiftPM, sorts them by target-relative
path, and generates `AdaScriptPluginsGenerated.swift` in the plugin work
directory. The generated plugin passes one source map to one
`AdaScriptPlugin`. Script source is embedded in the executable; the
original files are not read at runtime.
Install the generated plugin in your app scene:
Rebuilding the target after adding, removing, renaming, or editing an `.ada` file refreshes the generated source.

In a portable AdaScript project running in AdaEditor's macOS game window, edits
to `.ada` files hot reload after a short pause, including unsaved editor buffers.
The current ECS world remains active. A failed candidate leaves the last valid
code running and reports the error in Output. System instances and ordinary
script globals restart, and startup systems run once for the new version;
exported scriptable-object fields survive. Changes to
component, resource, network, or scriptable-object schemas require restarting
the game.

The same generated source contains native backing structs and registration for
scalar `@component` and `@resource` declarations. Because these declarations
change Swift layout, adding or editing their stored fields requires rebuilding
the target rather than source-only reload.
Register custom components
AdaScript resolves component names while plugins are set up. Register custom Swift components before the generated script plugin:

The `@Component` macro supplies field reflection for supported property types. A plain `Component` can participate in query matching, but its fields are not automatically available through the script bridge.
Load a script manually
Create an `AdaScriptPlugin` when you need control over the source location or loading failure:

You can also use `AdaScriptPlugin/init(source:name:)` when one source is
already in memory, or `AdaScriptPlugin/init(sources:name:)` with
`AdaScriptSource` values for a multi-file module. Script compilation,
import resolution, and annotation validation happen during initialization.
Native component resolution happens later during plugin setup.
Next steps
Read AdaScript Language for annotation syntax, then AdaScript ECS for queries, component fields, and native iterator behavior.

Use AdaScript syntax with AdaEngine declaration annotations. New to the
language? Start with AdaScript Basics for values, functions, types,
properties, control flow, asynchronous work, and annotations.
Source files

AdaScript uses `.ada` files. A file contains classes,
functions, variables, and control flow. AdaScript modules do not declare a
`main()` function and do not assemble plugin manifests.
Optional strict type checking

AdaScript remains dynamically typed by default. Enable strict checking for a
single source by placing `@strict` before its first declaration:

In an AdaEditor project, **Project Settings → Runtime → Type Checking → Strict**
enables the same analysis for every `.ada` source. The serialized setting is:

Strict checking validates annotated assignments, function arguments, member
access, and return values before the module runs. Use `Any` for an intentional
dynamic boundary. Untyped code and projects using `"dynamic"` keep normal
AdaScript runtime behavior.
Imports

Files with discovery annotations such as `@system` are module roots. Import a
helper declaration explicitly from another target-relative source file:

Relative imports are resolved from the importing file. The `.ada` extension is
optional. Absolute paths and imports which escape the Swift target source map
are rejected. A reachable source is compiled once, and an import cycle reports
the complete cycle.
Three import forms exist:

• `{ name }` imports a public declaration, and `name as Local` renames it for
  the importing file.
• `* as Alias` makes `Alias.name` refer to a public declaration of that file.
• `"AdaEngine"` and `"AdaUI"` are built-in modules. `AdaUI` has a closed list
  of views and rejects any other name. `AdaEngine` provides the script-facing
  services (`Input`, `Assets`, `Math`, `Vector3`, ...) and also accepts the
  components and resources the host registers at runtime, so those names are
  not checked statically.
• `"@library.id/path"` imports from a restored library.

A declaration is public unless written `private`. A private declaration is
module-local: importing it, or reaching it through a namespace, is an error, and
so is importing a name the file does not declare. Gravity compiles a module as
one global scope, so a name declared by two reachable files cannot coexist; the
duplicate is reported with both file names instead of being shadowed. Qualifying
a name with a namespace checks that it is exported but does not create a separate
scope. Imports are resolved by one parser and one set of path rules shared by the
runtime, the build generator, and the Editor, which also reports each import
cycle in full on every import that closes it and completes names inside
`import { | } from "module"`.
Annotations
AdaScript declaration annotations have three forms:

Arguments are compile-time constants or symbolic identifiers. They do not run
user code during module discovery.

See AdaScript Annotation Reference for supported annotations, declaration targets,
arguments, defaults, and lifetimes. An annotation the engine does not define, or
one placed on a target it does not support, is a compile error carrying the
file, line and column of the annotation. A one-time world initializer is a
`@system(scheduler: "startup")` class with `update(context)`; there is no
function-level `@init` annotation yet.
Script-defined data

The build plugin generates native backing types for scalar component and
resource schemas:

Component and resource fields may also be vectors, colors, enumerations, entity
references, and asset paths. The declared type selects the kind and the default
must match it:

Scripts read and write these as lists (`row.body.position[0]`,
`row.body.position = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]`) and strings; a write with the wrong length,
a non-finite number, or an unknown enum case is rejected and leaves the field
unchanged. These field kinds are not allowed in network fields. `aliases` keeps
scenes saved under a former name loadable: scenes are stored under the stable ID,
and `AdaScriptSceneSchemaResolver` reports a scene that still uses an alias,
fields that were removed, and values of the wrong type.

Generated Swift symbol names are private implementation details. Runtime lookup
accepts both the AdaScript declaration name (`Health`) and the stable ID
(`game.health`). `autoInsert: true` inserts the resource before systems are
installed. SwiftPM targets use generated backing types; AdaEditor can register
supported runtime-defined component layouts for pure AdaScript projects.

Bind a resource directly on a system with `@res`. The binding uses a native ECS
resource pointer during `update(context)`; field writes update the resource
change tick:

A missing required resource is reported through plugin diagnostics. Optional
resources can be guarded with `available()`:

A `@res` binding requests the scheduler access its use needs. It is read-only
when every use is a field read (`balance.acceleration`, `balance.available()`);
assigning a field, or any use that could alias the binding such as passing it or
storing it in another variable, requests write access. State the access
explicitly with `@res(access: "read")` or `@res(access: "write")`; declaring
`"read"` for a binding the system writes is a compile error. Two systems that only
read a resource may run at the same time.
World commands

Systems receive a capability-scoped world facade. Structural changes are
queued through `context.world.commands` and applied only after the current
system parameters finish, so an active query iterator cannot be invalidated:

The initial command API creates registered component defaults by AdaScript name
or stable ID:

Direct command use is inferred per system and declares deferred-world access to
the scheduler. Command facades expire when `update(context)` returns; using a
retained or undeclared facade reports a plugin diagnostic and performs no
mutation. Typed component constructors, including field overrides, can be passed
to `context.world.spawn([...])`, `commands.spawn([...])`, and
`commands.insert(entity, Component(...))`; the string-based form remains
available.
Dynamic access with `@access`

A system that needs to read or write a component by name, without declaring a
query, lists the components up front:

The declaration is added to the system's scheduler access, so the system never
runs concurrently with a conflicting one. Reading or writing a component outside
the set, or writing a read-only component, reports a diagnostic and does nothing.
Without `@access`, `read`, `write` and `has` are rejected.
Events

`@eventWriter(Name)` and `@events(Name)` bind an event writer and the received
events of one name to a system property:

The payload is a flat list of alternating field names and primitive values, which
keeps every queued value detached from the VM. A reader sees the events written
during the previous frame. Events require `EventsPlugin` (installed by the default
plugins); a system that declares them without it fails to install.
Exclusive world access

`@exclusiveWorld` marks a system that may change world structure immediately,
intended for startup, loading and tooling:

An exclusive system never runs alongside another system. An immediate operation
is rejected while one of the system's query iterators is still active.
Immediate resource insertion is not available yet.

SwiftPM generation of native backing types requires `AdaScriptBuildPlugin`;
supported pure AdaScript layouts can be registered by the runtime.

Swift and Editor tooling can attach the generated default without naming its
private backing type:
world.insertDefaultComponent(named: "game.health", into: entity.id)

Field types and serialization support vary by schema and bridge. Check the
nearest compiler diagnostic when a constructor argument or field default is
unsupported.
Scriptable objects

Use `@scriptable` for low-cardinality behavior attached to one entity. Systems
remain the scalable path for processing large entity sets.

The build plugin registers stable IDs, versions, aliases, exported scalar
defaults, and transient component/resource bindings. Required components are
checked before `ready`. Optional resources expose `available()`.

`ScriptableComponents` encodes a polymorphic envelope containing only `type`,
`version`, and detached `payload`. Entity bindings, resources, VM instances,
world contexts, and lifecycle state are never serialized. Decoding does not run
gameplay; attachment runs `ready` once and detachment runs `destroy` once.

Scriptable contexts expose the same expiring deferred commands facade as
systems. Retaining it after a callback produces a diagnostic. Scriptable
objects intentionally have no user-interface callback; compose interfaces in
Swift with AdaUI.
Multiplayer schemas

Use a typed command for peer intent. Field tags, rather than declaration order
or source names, define the wire schema:

Peers send the generated value through the scoped multiplayer resource. Host
systems receive typed values and an authenticated transport source:

The runtime owns packet sequences and command envelopes. `message.source`
cannot be supplied by script payload data. Swift and AdaScript declarations
with matching IDs, versions, tags, types, direction, delivery, and channel
produce the same compatibility schema.

`@replicated_component` uses `@network_field` plus optional `@local` fields.
SwiftPM targets receive a generated native ECS backing component through
`AdaScriptBuildPlugin`. Portable AdaEditor projects register each component as
a distinct runtime ECS layout without compiling Swift.
`@rpc` declares both a typed wire command and an optional receiver method:

Calling `input(...)` constructs a typed command; `multiplayer.send(...)` sends
it. The authored body does not run on the sender. On receipt, the system invokes
it before `update`, with `source` bound to the authenticated transport peer ID.
Fields remain tagged and require constant defaults. An empty or bodyless method
still works as a command constructor; `@remote_commands(input)` remains available
for explicit message processing. Request/response and local echo are not yet
supported.
Asynchronous work

Declare a function that can suspend with `async func`. Use `await` inside that
function; a synchronous action starts it explicitly with `Tasks.start(...)`.
The action returns immediately while the game or UI continues updating.

`Assets.loadAsync` and `Assets.saveAsync` use the native asset registry and
return an awaitable result. `Saves.writeAsync("@user://save.txt", text)` writes
an immutable string in the background and reports `committed()` after its
atomic file replacement. For data that cannot be copied in one callback, use
bounded chunks:

Each chunk is limited to 256 KiB. The writer appends to a temporary file and
replaces the destination only after `finishAsync()` succeeds. Build large ECS
snapshots in bounded pieces; do not retain a query row or live component view
in a task.

Mark a script-owned type with `@nonsendable` when its instances are tied to a
callback or another short lifetime. AdaScript rejects a typed async parameter
or method that would capture that type. Before a task starts, the runtime also
checks actual arguments, nested lists, returned values, and promise results;
this catches borrowed engine values passed through an untyped alias. Maps are
conservatively rejected until their entries can be inspected. See
AdaScript Annotation Reference.

`await Time.sleep(seconds)` advances with the scheduler's `deltaTime` and stops
advancing when that scheduler is paused. AdaEngine does not yet expose a
separate game time-scale resource.
`await Time.sleepRealTime(seconds)` uses a monotonic clock; continuation still
waits for a script dispatch point. `Tasks.promise()` creates a one-shot wait
that another script callback can resolve with `complete(value)`.
`Tasks.start(...)` returns a handle with `status()` and `cancel()`.

AdaScript callbacks such as `update(context)` remain synchronous. Do not mark
them `async`; start a separate async function and pass
detached values. Callback contexts, queries, resources, and commands expire at
callback exit. Awaited work resumes in the serialized script runtime, not on
the native I/O worker. Cancelling a save does not roll back
a file that was already committed.

Fallible operations return a result with `isSuccess()`, `value()`,
`errorCode()`, and `message()`; inspect it after `await`. A script VM trap
currently stops that module and cancels its pending tasks. Diagnostics include
the failing task, owner, and trace ID; reload the module to continue. Other
module instances and native gameplay remain separate.
System context

`update(context)` receives a scoped system context. `context.deltaTime` is the
current scheduler delta. Context and query values must not be retained after
the callback.

Common language patterns

The syntax primer in AdaScript Basics covers functions, conditions,
loops, structs, classes, static members, initializers, and accessors. In an ECS
system, use those language features together with query bindings:

Functions called by a system are ordinary helpers; they do not become
scheduler callbacks. A system's `update(context)` is the entry point selected
by `@system`. A scriptable object's `ready(context)` instead belongs to that
entity's attachment lifecycle. For one-time world setup, use the `startup`
scheduler described in AdaScript Annotation Reference.

An `import { name } from "./Helpers";` brings a helper into the target-level
module. Importing a file does not create a second world or a second run of its
systems. A library can contribute its own annotated declarations; keep IDs
unique across the assembled module. See AdaScript Libraries.
Values crossing the bridge

AdaScript bridge values are detached booleans, integers, finite floating-point
numbers, strings, lists, and null. ECS component views are borrowed native
capabilities rather than detached values.

Unsupported values and invalid numeric conversions are rejected without
partially mutating a component.

System `update(context)` callbacks are command-style. Their return values are
ignored; observable behavior belongs in components, resources, events, or
diagnostics.
Declare annotation-driven systems and iterate native AdaECS component columns.
Declare a system
Apply `@system` to a class and implement `update(context)`:

The scheduler defaults to `update`. System identifiers must be unique within a
script module.

For one-time world setup, use `@system(scheduler: "startup")`. Its
`update(context)` runs on the default scheduler runner's first update, before
the regular frame stages. A script class constructor does not receive a world
context. See AdaScript Annotation Reference for all annotation arguments.
Order systems

Use repeatable `@after` and `@before` annotations when component and resource
access alone does not express the required execution order:

Dependency IDs resolve within the same AdaScript module. Both systems must use
the same scheduler. AdaScript rejects unknown IDs, self-dependencies, and
dependency cycles while loading the module.
Declare a query
Apply `@query` to a stored system property:

Positional components are fetched and available on each row. Four more clauses
take one component or a list:

| Clause | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `optional: Target` | Fetched like a positional component, but rows may lack it. `entity.target` is `null` when absent. |
| `with: Movable` | The entity must have it; it is not fetched. |
| `without: Frozen` | The entity must not have it. |
| `changed: Health` | Rows where any listed component changed since the system last ran. |
| `added: Marker` | Rows where any listed component was added since the system last ran. |

`changed` and `added` need the component to exist in the archetype; the change tick
of a component is updated by every successful field write. A boolean `where:` clause
and any other label are rejected with a message naming the supported clauses.

Row properties are the lower-camel-case component names, or an explicit alias
written with `as`. A component may be named by its qualified path:

Two fetched components with the same short name (`Game.Health` and `Physics.Health`)
are an error until one is given an alias, and no component may be aliased `id`.
`entity.id` exposes the native entity identifier.
Iterator behavior

AdaScript queries are native iterators. AdaECS resolves matching archetypes,
binds component columns when entering a chunk, and advances their pointers by
row stride. The bridge does not create an entity proxy for every result and
does not perform a world component lookup for every field access.

A query row and its component views are borrowed. Do not retain them after the
loop or system update returns. Structural changes must use deferred commands.
Inactive entities are skipped. Empty queries execute zero loop iterations.
Component fields

The `@Component` Swift macro generates the runtime field accessors used by Ada
Script. Register native components before the script plugin is set up.

Supported field values include booleans, integers, finite floating-point
values, strings, vectors, quaternions, colors, and reflected enums. A rejected
write leaves the component unchanged and appends a development diagnostic.
Access planning

The compiler reads how a system uses its rows and requests exactly that access
from the scheduler:

var current = entity.health.current;   // read Health
entity.health.current = current - 1;   // write Health
entity.health.current -= 1;            // read and write Health

A component that is only read can be shared with other readers; a write reserves
it exclusively. `changed:` and `added:` read a component's ticks, so they request
read access even for a component that is not fetched. Filter-only components
(`with`, `without`) request none.

Analysis follows `for (var row in query)` loops. If a row, a component view, or the
query itself escapes into code the compiler cannot follow (passed to a function,
stored, called with an unknown method), the system must declare what it touches:

Without `@access` this fails to compile, naming the query and component. A
declaration may be broader than the code but not narrower: declaring a component
read-only while the script writes it is an error. The same `@access` declaration
governs the dynamic `context.world.read/write` calls. A precompiled module has no
script text to analyse and keeps write access to every fetched component.

Project input actions

In **Project Settings → Input Bindings**, add an action such as `Jump`, then add
keyboard, mouse, gamepad or touch bindings. Click **Save Project Settings**.
Actions are stored in `.ada/project.json` and loaded by both Play Mode and the
AdaScript project runtime. Multiple bindings act as alternatives: releasing one
input does not release the action while another binding is held.

Systems and scriptable components declare input as a read-only resource dependency
with `@res var input: Input;`. Only declarations that request Input receive it.
Use `@res(optional: true) var input: Input;` and `input.available()` when the
resource may be absent; a missing required resource produces a diagnostic.

• `isActionPressed(name)` remains true while an input is held.
• `isActionJustPressed(name)` and `isActionJustReleased(name)` describe transitions
  during the current frame. Both can be true for a tap completed within one frame.
• `getActionStrength(name)` returns 0...1. Gamepad axes use a direction and the
  action's dead zone; buttons and touch return either zero or one.
• Gamepad bindings match any connected controller. `Any Finger Held` stays active
  until every contact ends or is cancelled. Touch lifecycle events, mouse motion,
  and wheel bindings produce frame pulses.

Input snapshots are scoped to a callback; query input again on the next update.
Unknown action names return false or zero. Names are case-sensitive.

Swift systems use the same methods on their `Input` resource. `InputPlugin()`
loads the `inputActions` section from `.ada/project.json` in the current working
directory, including games launched from the editor. Packaged Swift applications
can decode `[InputAction]` from an included resource and pass it to
`InputPlugin(actions:)`, or call `try input.setInputActions(actions)` on an existing
resource. Explicit `InputPlugin(actions: [])` disables automatic project loading.

Understand annotation, setup, and runtime failures and keep ECS work on the
native chunk path.
Compilation diagnostics

`AdaScriptPlugin` compiles the source and reads declaration metadata
without executing a `main()` manifest. Initialization throws
`AdaScriptError/compilation(_:)` for syntax or semantic errors and
`AdaScriptError/invalidManifest(_:)` for invalid AdaEngine annotations.

Examples include `@system` on a non-class declaration, duplicate system
identifiers, `@query` outside a system class, a query with no fetched
components, and a system class that cannot be initialized.
Setup diagnostics

Native component identifiers are resolved during plugin setup so earlier
plugins can register game components. Unknown or ambiguous component names skip
the affected system and append a diagnostic.
Runtime diagnostics

Runtime diagnostics include unknown component aliases, unknown fields,
unsupported values, invalid numeric conversions, and query capabilities used
outside their callback lifetime.

Inspect `AdaScriptPlugin/diagnostics` after setup and during development.
System `update(context)` callbacks are command-style; their return values are
ignored. Tests should assert observable ECS state and diagnostics.
Performance model

AdaScript query execution traverses native archetypes and chunks. Component
columns are bound once per chunk, and field access advances a typed pointer by
row stride. A successful write mutates the component in place and updates its
change tick.

The hot path avoids arrays of matched entity identifiers, one Swift bridge
object per entity, repeated entity-location lookups, existential component
copies, and whole-component reinsertion.

The current embedded C runtime is globally shared and non-reentrant, so runtime entry remains
serialized. Scalability comes from native filtering, column iteration, cached
metadata, and narrow bridge calls rather than multiple concurrent VMs.

Benchmark scripting changes with multiple archetypes and chunks and compare
them with a typed Swift query. Validate semantics before drawing performance
conclusions.

The mobile agent and desktop editor MCP share native model tools and offline knowledge. Start with `editor.project.context`; its `model3D` field describes formats, tools and verification limits. Desktop context also lists `authoringTools`. Tools require an open project on desktop and operate inside the project's declared Assets root. Import sources may also be under project-local Downloads.
Inspect and validate

`editor.model.inspect` and `editor.model.validate` accept a project-relative `path`, such as `Assets/Models/Robot.glb`. Both run the production `NativeGLTFLoader` without constructing GPU resources. They report geometry counts, selected-scene rest-pose bounds at the original scale, material indexes and PBR factors, texture/image mappings, nodes, skin joints, named clips and durations, and local dependencies. Large inventories are bounded and marked `truncated`.

Validation checks dependency containment and byte budgets, native decoding, image decoding, scene hierarchy, primitive geometry and the current import profile. `editor.asset.validate` also routes GLB/glTF to this validation. This is not a complete Khronos conformance check, GPU rendering proof or animation-playback proof. It does not author or validate gameplay collision shapes.

This profile supports glTF 2.0 primitive topologies, UV0/UV1, one set of four skin influences and at most 128 joints per skin. Required Draco/Meshopt/KTX2 extensions are unsupported. Node TRS and morph-weight clips can use LINEAR, STEP and CUBICSPLINE interpolation. Models and their local dependencies have a combined 128 MiB budget. JSON and decoded accessor inventories have additional bounds.
Import and place

Call `editor.model.import` with `source: "Downloads/Robot/Robot.gltf"` and `destination: "Assets/Models"`. Validation runs before copying. Local buffers/textures are copied as one portable bundle; repeated imports choose new names and preserve existing files. Network references, missing dependencies and escaping paths/symlinks fail. The tool returns the imported `path` and `assetReference`.

Read `editor.components.describe` with query `Model3DSource`. Its `source` uses the returned `@res://` reference. Keep the required Transform and use its scale intentionally. For simple playback, set the exact inspected `animation` name, `autoplay` and `repeats`. Preserve unrelated fields, including any project-authored animation graph. When `animationGraph` is present it takes precedence over the single `animation` clip; do not silently discard it to force clip playback. Pose-graph editing is distinct from skeletal keyframe/rig authoring.

Desktop agents should use `editor.scene.get/apply` with the latest revision to place models in open scenes and retain document undo. Mobile agents use their project file tools for scene YAML. Imported meshes do not automatically receive physics bodies or colliders; read the PhysicsBody3DComponent descriptor before adding one.
Materials and lighting

`editor.model.material.edit` accepts `path`, zero-based `material` and `settingsJSON`. Supported patch keys are `baseColorFactor` (linear RGBA), `metallicFactor`, `roughnessFactor`, `emissiveFactor` (linear RGB), `alphaMode`, `alphaCutoff` and `doubleSided`. Invalid patches fail before writing. Unpatched material fields, hierarchy, animation data and GLB binary chunks are preserved.

`editor.model.texture.assign` binds an image to `baseColor`, `normal`, `metallicRoughness`, `emissive` or `occlusion`. Inspect material indexes first. glTF roughness uses G and metallic uses B; normal and material maps are linear data, while base-color/emission textures are sRGB. `editor.texture.render` can create procedural placeholders and flat normal maps. These operations do not unwrap a mesh or bake lighting. Editing a shared model asset affects all references to it; rebuild/reload before comparing appearance.

Read exact Camera, Mesh3DComponent, light, Environment3D and physics payloads from `editor.components.describe`. Camera framing, lighting, model scale and valid UVs all matter. Use the `basic-3d-scene` example for a perspective camera, PBR cube, directional light and game3d plugin configuration.
Knowledge and verification

`editor.skills.list` returns bundled workflow descriptions; `editor.skills.read` loads instructions by ID. The 3D packs are `ada-3d-assets`, `ada-3d-materials` and `ada-3d-animation`. Their detailed instructions are loaded when needed. `editor.docs.search/read`, `editor.api.describe`, `editor.components.describe` and `editor.examples.list/read` also work offline on both hosts.

Desktop uses `editor.build.start`, `editor.play.start`, `editor.task.status`, `editor.output.read`, `editor.play.capture` / `render.capture_screenshot` (the running game's camera frame; the editor window is returned only when no game runs, and is not evidence) and `editor.play.run_scenario` for scripted input, frames and state. Mobile uses `editor.build`, `editor.play.start`, `editor.play.capture` and `editor.image.read`. Select the tools actually advertised by the current host. Desktop asset tools exclude mobile vision analysis and direct on-disk scene assignment; desktop scene edits go through the revision/undo workflow. Save dirty asset documents before tool writes.

After validation and build, inspect a completed frame from visible Play. A 3D scene needs a camera, a light and an `Environment3D` (or a camera `backgroundColor`/clear flags) so the frame is not a flat clear color; `editor.play.run_scenario` can capture before/after frames around input. Exercise selected clips and compare frames at different times for animation. Isolated simulation verifies logic and keyboard/physics behavior; it does not install Model3D or prove rendering. Native desktop agents can create/extract and edit skeletal/morph clips using the revision-checked `editor.animation.*` API; read [Animation authoring](AnimationAuthoring.md) for explicit Save, scene binding, shared Tool API 2, budgets and verification. Query `animationAuthoring` in desktop project context before use; mobile hosts do not advertise these desktop authoring commands. Blender execution, visual rig-structure editing and automatic rig inference remain unavailable. To create a new low-poly model use editor.model.generate (an AdaScript program that writes a GLB) or editor.voxel.generate (a .vox).

NPC configuration workflow

Ask: “Create an interactive NPC configuration form, then generate an editable
dialog preview from my submitted values.” The bundled `/ada-ui-forms` skill
provides the workflow to agents that need more explicit guidance.

1\. The assistant streams a form inside its reply. Edit its fields and toggles.
2\. After the agent's turn finishes, submit the form. Submission returns the
   current values to the same ACP session; an unsent composer draft is preserved.
3\. The agent returns a new preview surface. Click **Open in UI Designer** to
   create a new project-local `.ui` asset and open it in the normal workbench.
4\. Refine through the designer's controls or YAML view, use undo/redo, and save.

Export paths are `Assets/UI/AgentPreviews/<surface>-<unique-id>.ui`; each export
creates a new file, and symlinked destination directories are rejected. The
snapshot retains native components, bindings with current defaults, and named
host actions. It does not serialize the agent transport or action-context mapping.
Transport contract

Studio advertises its custom catalog and compact component contract in ACP prompt
context. Ordinary assistant text remains Markdown. A fenced `a2ui` block contains
one complete JSON envelope per line; complete lines render progressively.
An exact opening fence at the end of a prose line is accepted too, because some
ACP agents concatenate planner and final replies without an intervening newline.
Fences inside ordinary code blocks remain ordinary text.
ACP embedded resources using `application/vnd.a2ui+json` or
`application/a2ui+json` are also accepted. This is an ACP text/resource binding;
it does not require a new ACP extension or a second MCP server.

The catalog supports Text, Row, Column, Button, TextField, Toggle, a single-string
ChoicePicker, and numeric Slider, with absolute JSON Pointer bindings and server
event actions. Required/range checks show inline errors and disable invalid
submit buttons. Checks and controls survive the `.ui` authoring handoff.
It does not advertise the Basic Catalog, executable code, general/local functions, collection templates, or
arbitrary modifiers. See the engine's `Documentation/A2UI.md` for schema details.

Button actions become an `[A2UI user action]` context block on the next prompt
in the owning conversation, including the envelope and its transport metadata.
`sendDataModel` sends only the originating surface's model. Other conversations
and other configured agents cannot receive a surface's submission. Changing
providers disables older forms until their original agent is reconnected.

Malformed interfaces show an inline error while retaining the previous working
surface. Correction feedback accompanies the following prompt. Interrupted or
failed runs have explicit surface states. Updates to a submitted surface can
make it ready for another interaction; a completed one-shot form stays submitted.

The ACP adapter waits for all session notifications preceding a prompt response
to reach the transcript before marking the turn complete. This handles bursty
streams and slow UI rendering without a timing-based completion delay.
Persistence and scope

Compact surface state, including locally edited values, is saved in the existing
project chat session store. Switching chats preserves each live surface instance;
reopening Studio reconstructs surfaces without replaying server defaults over
local edits. Incomplete in-flight forms reopen as interrupted. Existing sessions
without the new optional field remain readable.

Inspection memory

Large Swift generic view types can expand into huge diagnostic names. UI inspection
now reports a bounded nominal type name from immutable Swift runtime descriptors,
with generic arguments omitted. This avoids constructing the reflected/mangled
name tree. In the development fixture run, sampled RSS ranged from 333 to 567 MiB and settled near 337 MiB;
this is macOS workflow evidence, not a universal leak or performance guarantee.
Configured-agent context limits

when the selected model has no context-window metadata and the runtime falls back

Short, working patterns for input, movement, spawning, collisions, score, restart and sound in AdaScript games.

The complete game that uses all of them is the bundled example `side-scroller-3d`: a 3D side-scroller in about twenty small files with a scene, a HUD, sounds and tests. Find it with `editor.examples.list` (query "3D game", "side scroller", "flappy" or "runner") and read it with `editor.examples.read`. Blocks marked `// recipe` below are compiled by Studio's test suite, so they are safe to copy. Studio's pure AdaScript projects accept `@resource` structs, bound with `@res`; the example nevertheless keeps shared data (round state, intent, cues) in `@component` structs on one "Game" entity in the scene, read with `@query`, so the scene can author it and tests can read it. Syntax follows ADR-0001 to ADR-0003 (annotations and modules, ECS queries, components and resources); see AdaScript ECS and AdaScript Language.
Lay the game out in files

One responsibility per file, grouped by layer: `Config.ada` (all balance numbers), `Rules.ada` (pure functions), `Components/` (data only), `Systems/` (one `@system` per file), `UI/`, `Tests/`, `Generators/` (asset generator sources as `.txt`, not compiled). Import across files with `import { Name } from "./Path.ada";`. Systems are ordered with `@before(id:)` and `@after(id:)`. Do not write a game as one file.
Input

Declare actions (name and bindings such as Space, left mouse button, touch) in project settings; they are stored in `.ada/project.json`. Bind the `Input` resource in exactly one system (`@res(optional: true)` with an `available()` check, so tests can run it without `Input`) and publish what the player asked for as a component on the Game entity. The other systems read that component, which keeps them testable because tests have no `Input`.

`isActionPressed` is true while held, `isActionJustPressed` and `isActionJustReleased` are single-frame transitions, `getActionStrength` is 0 to 1. Action names are case sensitive; an unknown name is false or zero.
Movement and gravity

Components hold state; the position is the entity's `Transform`. Read `position` as a list and write a whole list back. Scale all motion by `context.deltaTime`, clamped so a long frame cannot skip over a collision.
Put balance numbers in a `Config` class (`static var`), never in the systems.
Spawning and removing entities

Structural changes go through `context.world.commands` and are applied after the system finishes. `spawn([...])` takes component constructors; `despawn(entity.id)` removes an entity. A query row is borrowed: use it inside the loop, do not store it.

Mesh and material components cannot be constructed from a script, so anything with a visible 3D mesh is authored in the scene. Scroll a **pool** of scene entities and reuse them instead of spawning: when an obstacle leaves the screen, move it to the back of the line and give it a new gap (`ObstacleSystem` in the example). Spawn and despawn suit logic-only entities and entities built from components a script can construct.
Collisions and scoring

Keep the geometry in a pure function and the reaction in a system. For a side view, test the circle or box against columns in x and y. Score a column once, with a `passed` flag on the obstacle component, and raise a cue for sound.
Two queries in one system can be nested (`for (var a in as) { for (var b in bs) { ... } }`). Pass numbers into functions, not rows.
Phases, game over and restart

Store the round in a component on the Game entity: `phase` (ready, playing, over), `score`, `best` and a `resetRequested` flag. One system changes the phase from the intent; another system performs the reset when the flag is set (positions, velocities, score, flags), then clears the flag. A reset flag that starts `true` also places everything on the first frame. Gameplay systems return early unless the phase is playing.
Sound with AudioSource

Create the sound with `editor.audio.generate`, add one entity per sound in the scene with an `AudioSource` (`source: "@res://Audio/flap.wav"`) and a small marker component carrying the cue name. Systems raise a cue flag in a component on the Game entity; one audio system sets `audioSource.play = true` on the matching entity and clears the cues. The engine clears `play` itself. Use one entity per sound that can overlap itself, because a second `play` restarts the first.
HUD

Author the HUD as a `.ui` file with string inputs, add a `UIComponent` entity that points to it, and bind each input to an exported field of a `@scriptable` class with `scriptBindings`. A scriptable can bind a script-defined `@component` with `@component var state: GameState;` and read it in `update(context)`. The example instead has one system write the text into a small `static var` presentation model (`HudModel`) that the scriptable copies into its exported fields. Gameplay never reads the model. Keep the wording in a pure function so tests can check it.
Test the game without a window

Choose the project build system

In standalone desktop Studio, open **Project Settings → Project** and choose
**AdaScript** or **SwiftPM** under **Build System**. **Save Project Settings**
applies the choice to the whole project and all its named build targets. SwiftPM
requires a `Package.swift` in the project root with an executable product.

For example, a SwiftPM manifest can declare
`.executableTarget(name: "MyGame", path: "Native")`. Add a Swift entry point in
`Native/`, then choose **SwiftPM** and save. In the project navigator,
**Targets** shows `MyGame` and the source files SwiftPM assigns to it, including
files in custom directories. Use **Files** to browse the full project.

On the local desktop, **Run** starts the Swift executable. A Swift AdaEngine
app can open its first window in its `@main` app code without any `.ascn` file.
If the package has several executables, choose **Executable Product** in
**Edit Build Targets…**. The optional editor scene is used for scene editing
and scene Play. AdaScript projects use the configured scene, root view, or
startup system.
Named build targets

The shared desktop toolbar shows a build-target picker next to the run platform.
Choose **Edit Build Targets…** to create, duplicate, rename or delete targets.
Each target stores its startup scene, Debug/Release configuration, run destination,
arguments, source inclusion/exclusion, resource roots and runtime/plugin settings.
For example, use a Debug target starting at a test scene and a Release target
starting at the game's main scene. Save selects the target open in the editor;
Cancel discards the entire draft. The last target cannot be deleted. Switching is
disabled during builds, running games, debugging, player deployment or recording.

Targets persist in `.ada/project.json` as `buildTargets` with `activeBuildTargetID`.
Existing projects retain their settings and need no migration. Opening the target
editor prepares a Main target from those settings; only Save writes it to disk.
Activating a target projects its settings onto the ordinary `build`, `run`,
`runtime`, `editor.startupScene` and `paths.resourceRoots` fields, so existing
Play/build/export/CLI consumers use the same active configuration. Ordinary
Project Settings saves update the active target. Project identity, input actions,
engine paths and AI settings remain shared. SwiftPM targets also remember the
executable product and apply file/resource selection through the manifest editor.
Game diagnostics overlay

In **Edit Build Targets…**, turn on **Diagnostics overlay** for a local desktop
target, save, and run that target. FPS and frame time appear in the top-left of
the game window. The readout passes input through to the game. It shows update
cadence and mean time between updates, including stalls.

The flag defaults to off. Duplicate a target to copy its value. You can keep one
target for everyday play and enable diagnostics on a separate performance
target. The setting applies to local AdaScript and compatible Swift product
runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux, in Debug and Release. Swift apps need a
version of AdaEngine with overlay support and a standard `DefaultAppWindow`
or `WindowGroup`. Other destinations keep the saved flag for future desktop
runs.

AdaScript source inclusion/exclusion applies to project sources in local builds
and native exports; library dependencies remain included. Paths are relative to
the project. This does not prune assets or scenes from the exported asset folder.
Native macOS/Web/Android toolbar exports use a stable per-target subdirectory
under `Exports/<platform>/` so targets do not replace each other's output. Toolchain
requirements and supported export platforms are unchanged. The browser shell and
dedicated phone screens do not yet expose the target editor.

Load the bundled `ada-build-run` skill for target configuration. Inspect the open

targets are not platform destinations or SwiftPM executable products. To verify
the selected target use `editor.play.start` with `mode: "product"`; scene mode
instead runs the active scene document.

There is no dedicated desktop MCP tool for creating or selecting named targets.
Use the target editor, or available project file tools with the following rules:

• Preserve the schema version, unknown fields, unrelated targets and stable IDs.
  When adding the first target, copy the existing effective project settings.
• Before switching externally, capture the outgoing top-level settings in its
  current target. Set the new `activeBuildTargetID` and project the selected
  target's fields together: `build` → `build`, `run` → `run`, `runtime` → `runtime`,
  `startupScene` → `editor.startupScene`, and `resourceRoots` → `paths.resourceRoots`.

• When changing a scene entry, update both the target's `runtime.entry.scene`
  and `startupScene`, plus the active projection. Keep `product` on its target;

• Target names must be nonempty and unique ignoring case; IDs must be nonempty
  and unique. All targets use the project's build system. Configuration is
  `debug` or `release`. Validation checks inactive targets too.
• Include/exclude paths match files or directory prefixes relative to the project,
  not wildcard patterns. Empty includes mean all project sources; exclusions win.
  Include the project sources imported by the entry code.
• Stop active project tasks and save dirty documents before external edits.
  Reload the project afterwards so the toolbar and workspace agree with disk.

or build through the editor and read its diagnostics. The CLI `--target` flag is
an export platform selector, not a named-target selector. Finally run the product
and verify its startup scene; metadata/build validation alone is not runtime proof.

Open a native Studio scene and select **Terrain** in the viewport toolbar. The
terrain dock opens **below the viewport**. It includes **Sculpt**, **Materials**,
**Joining**, **Mesh Instancing**, and **Height Generator**. The Inspector keeps
ordinary entity components. **Mesh Instancing** also has its own viewport toolbar
button. Play uses a separate runtime and does not show the authoring dock.
Create and join Mesh Terrain

Set **Terrain Type** to **Mesh Terrain** and choose **Create Terrain**. This
creates a saved 128-unit surface from a 64 Ã— 64 grid of cells. Choose **Heightfield**
to create ground for the heightfield workflow described below.

For a first join, add a static cube to the scene and position it so it crosses the
ground surface. In **Joining**, select the cube, choose the **Target Terrain**, set
**Operation** to **Join**, and choose **Join selected mesh**. A closed mesh with
consistent face winding works as a solid. Joining replaces the overlapping faces
with a connected surface. The cube stays in the hierarchy and remains selectable.
A self-contained GLB can contribute its opaque trunk and roots while its
cutout leaves keep their own draw. Joined source triangles keep the original
color, roughness, normal maps and texture coordinates. Keep the model in
project Assets so the joined surface can load its textures when you reopen the
scene.

Use **Contact width** to control the transition around a joined object. Choose
**Subtract** to cut a closed shape out of the terrain, or **Conform** to project
the existing ground toward a static mesh. Conform keeps the source visible and
works with an open surface. **Projection distance** limits the reach of the
projection above and below the ground; **Projection strength** controls how far
the affected vertices move. Choose **Apply operation** to rebuild.

Select the cube and use the viewport's Move tool. While the editor prepares a new
surface, the previous terrain remains visible. Releasing saves the accepted shape
and position in one Undo step. Escape cancels an in-progress move. Undo and Redo
restore the saved surface with the cube's corresponding position. The original
model asset stays available for reuse. Keep the entire joined mesh within the
terrain's boundary. A move past the edge is rejected and the last accepted
position stays in the scene.

To place a joined object precisely, edit its Transform in the Inspector and
press Enter. The terrain and the object's new transform are saved together.
If the new position crosses the terrain boundary, Studio keeps the last valid
position and shows why the edit was rejected.

To move a group of joined objects, select their parent in the hierarchy. All
joined objects in the group must share one Mesh Terrain target. Release the
Move handle or press Enter in the Inspector to save the group and the rebuilt
terrain in one Undo step.

Select the bound object and choose **Detach from terrain** in Joining or in the
Inspector to make it independent again. The ground and its procedural population
rebuild without that object. Undo restores the original binding and surface.

Use the render selector in the 3D viewport to choose **Wireframe** or **Shaded +
Wireframe**. Wireframe shows triangle edges; the combined mode keeps the shaded
surface visible under the edges. Choose **Shaded** to return to the usual view.
These modes are for inspection in the viewport and do not change Play or the
scene's authored materials.

Zoom out in Wireframe to inspect Mesh Terrain's render LOD. Eligible regions
switch to a coarser meshlet level as they occupy fewer pixels. Adjacent terrain
sections keep the same shared edge, even when one section shows finer triangles.
Regions with varying material paint retain their original triangles.
Create and generate heightfield ground

With **Terrain Type** set to **Heightfield**, **Create Terrain** creates a saved
128-unit terrain with 129 Ã— 129 height samples under an Environment parent. The
resource lives in project Assets. In **Height
Generator**, set **Height Amplitude**, **Noise Frequency**, and the seed, then choose
**Generate Heightmap**. Five deterministic noise octaves create hills and valleys;
**New Seed** changes their arrangement. Generating on an existing source keeps its
other saved channels and creates one undoable resource version.

**Add region** expands a partial region before adding an adjacent 256-cell region.
The runtime uses 64-cell surface chunks, independent persistence regions, distance
LOD, and bounded streaming. Old heightfield Terrain components remain readable.
Sculpt in the viewport

Choose **Raise**, **Lower**, **Smooth**, or **Flatten**. On Mesh Terrain, Smooth
follows connected triangles on the selected surface. Flatten uses the plane at
the start of the stroke. The Heightfield workflow also offers presets for ramps,
terraces, noise, erosion and brush shapes. Radius and strength are shared
controls. Hold the left button and drag over visible terrain. A blue
ring follows its surface. Source strokes publish worker batches **while the button
is held**. Releasing finishes the stroke and saves one resource version; Escape
cancels it. Each complete stroke is one ordinary scene Undo action. Undo, Redo,
Save and reopening the scene retain the selected resource version.

Terrain authoring uses coherent asynchronous worker publication. Large volumetric
regions can take longer to prepare than a simple heightfield. The previous valid
mesh stays visible while a batch is prepared, and camera navigation remains usable.
Height tools edit the base heightfield; volume tools address additional strata.
Materials and texture variation

In **Materials**, choose a card to paint its layer. **Add Materialâ€¦** opens the
system file picker and imports a PNG or JPEG as a new layer, with a thumbnail.
Imported textures are copied into the terrain resource directory. Terrain layers
have stable IDs; choosing another card does not renumber saved paint.

**Automatic Grass / Rock / Snow** initializes height and slope rules. Grass covers
lower gentle ground, rock covers steeper surfaces, and snow covers higher ground.
Existing layers are retained when applying variation settings again. Painted
material overrides these rules; **Erase material paint** reveals them again.

On Mesh Terrain, select its entity in the hierarchy before painting. Each stroke
follows the connected side under the brush. Paint on the ground stays in place;
paint on a joined rock or root follows the source when it moves. If that part of
the surface disappears, the stroke stays saved and can apply again when a
matching surface returns. Erasing reveals the current contact and automatic
layers. Paint and erase each create one Undo step and leave the mesh shape alone.

New texture layers use deterministic flips, quarter-turn rotations, random offsets,
macro variation and triplanar projection. Terrain-local coordinates keep variation
stable across chunk boundaries and camera movement. Volume material fields evaluate
actual surface height and normal, including multiple strata at the same X/Z.
Mesh instancing and solids

Select the separate **Mesh Instancing** button, then **Add Meshâ€¦** to import a
self-contained GLB or VOX. Choose its palette entry, density and brush radius.
**Paint meshes** and **Erase meshes** edit persistent instance records. Copies share
mesh buffers rather than becoming thousands of authored hierarchy entities.
Decorative instances do not create per-instance physics bodies by default.

On Mesh Terrain, **Paint meshes** records where to generate the selected
prototype. **Erase meshes** clears its generated coverage without deleting
manual placements or pinned overrides. A pin that loses its supporting surface
is retained in the resource for recovery. If a joined object moves, the ground
it uncovers can grow the painted vegetation again. The area around its new
position clears according to the rule's exclusion distance.

**Add solid** and **Subtract solid** use a sphere, box, capsule or a registered
palette mesh as an ordered volume operation. Position it with the brush and release
to apply. Caves and overhangs are real generated surfaces, with matching runtime
collision. Mesh operands must be supported closed static solids. Self-contained
models avoid silently omitting external model dependencies. Invalid resources keep
the last valid terrain generation.
Saved sources and compatibility

An entity's **Terrain Source** component references a project `.aterrain` resource,
for example `@res://Terrain/playground.aterrain`. Keep its immutable region, mesh
document, model, texture and volume files together. The editing runtime resolves absolute paths;
scene references stay portable. Missing or outside-project terrain roots are rejected.

Strokes operate on private same-directory manifest versions and publish their URI
through scene history. Earlier resources remain exact for Undo; unpublished manifests
are removed only after active filesystem writers finish. Shared payloads are never
deleted by gesture cancellation. Intermediate versions can therefore accumulate.

The edit viewport omits source collision cooking; authored collision settings and
Play retain runtime physics. A nil streaming radius retains full-declared-set
residency, while newly added generic Source components use the engine's camera
streaming default. The old Terrain component still supports its four legacy brushes.
Advanced presets and saved palettes belong to Terrain Source resources.

Native Windows is exercised during development. Other platform acceptance and full
portable export validation remain separate checks; local editor tests do not prove
those platforms. Three-dimensional manual paint storage and volumetric curvature
rules are not yet equivalent to the heightfield paint channels.

Run through AdaMCP

Start a fresh `adastudio-flow --stdio` process with an AdaMCP-compatible Content-Length framed client. The repository contains a check that runs the example through both interfaces:
